near_miss.why_not: Lucretius' religio showing its head from the sky has nothing to do with the Norse kenning (head called sky/house of the brain); hǫfuð ~ caput is mere co-occurrence. See search lead for the real comparandum.

search_lead.cognate: none (motif, no cognate words: haus/hǫfuð vs śīrṣán-, himinn vs dyaúḥ)
search_lead.argument: The kenning 'head = sky (of the brain)' presupposes the cosmogonic skull-sky correspondence of the Ymir myth, which matches the Puruṣa hymn's sky from the head. A motif comparison, not phraseology.

near_miss.lead: vatn ~ ὕδωρ, kona ~ γυνή (women and water)
near_miss.why_not: Rígsþula's 'jósu vatni' is the naming lustration of a newborn, while Herodotus describes Scythian women's cosmetic paste. No shared context, and the cognates are basic vocabulary.

near_miss.lead: hear with the ears: eyra/heyra ~ οὖς/ἀκούω
near_miss.why_not: Cognate pair, but the collocation is universal, and Snorri treats it as a learned pleonasm, probably after Donatus (vocemque his auribus hausi). The Germanic hits found by search (eyru ... heyra, orun gihorent, mid is ôrun hôrid) are Biblical. Hesiod Th. 701 (οὔασι ὄσσαν ἀκοῦσαι) is also generic. Herodotus' thymos dwelling in the ears is a different figure.

near_miss.lead: segja ~ þegja / inquam ~ tacent (speak vs be silent, *teh2k-)
near_miss.why_not: þegja ~ tacere is a good equation, and Plautus has the same contrast elsewhere (Bacch. 35 ut tu taceas ego loquar), as does Hávamál (mæli þarft eða þegi). But speak-versus-be-silent is generic. The anchor contexts differ: a skald's call for his audience's silence, against a greeting met with silence. No Plautine prologue call for silence is in the corpus.
The equation is right, but the context is a grammatical gloss on pleonasm against a comic narrative. Generic.

near_miss.lead: tvenn vatna djúp ~ dvé śīrṣé (numeral dyads)
near_miss.why_not: Only numerals and 'new' (nýr/nor/nytt) co-occur; nothing collocational, and the Norse is Christian exegesis.

near_miss.lead: hlóð ek lofkǫst ... óbrotgjarn (the poem as a lasting built monument)
near_miss.why_not: The slab's partners (a Scythian sacrifice; Thucydides on thymos and ergon) are irrelevant, and verk ~ ἔργον is chance. The real comparandum lies outside the slab: see search lead.

search_lead.cognate: none (renewal: hlaða 'pile up' ~ τειχίζω 'wall'; lofkǫstr 'praise-cairn' ~ ὕμνων θησαυρός)
search_lead.argument: In both, the praise poem is a built structure, raised by the poet, that endures and is proof against destruction (lengi stendr óbrotgiarn ~ storm and wind will not destroy it). Horace's exegi monumentum (Odes 3.30, outside the corpus) belongs to the same topos, and the topos may be literary rather than inherited.

near_miss.lead: vindr ~ ventus with ship (skip dverga / nauis)
near_miss.why_not: 'Ship of the dwarves' is a kenning for poetry; Catullus has a real ship in a storm. Wind and ship together are generic.
In Haustlǫng bǫnd means 'the gods' (bǫnd ollu 'the gods caused it') and fló is flight, whereas AV has a boat floating away from its mooring rope. Two unrelated uses.

near_miss.lead: Svein ól móðir, silki vafði ~ kumāráṃ mātā́ ... sámubdham (mother + boy + *webʰ- 'wrap')
near_miss.why_not: Attractive: mother, male child (accusative) and a participle or verb that the lexicon maps to *webʰ-. But the *webʰ- membership of √ubh 'confine, hold together' is uncertain. RV 5.2.1 is about the hidden fire-child, not swaddling, and swaddling a newborn is a generic birth-scene detail (Rígsþula repeats it for every birth).
The same two roots are juxtaposed in both, but in different relations: in Norse the boy grows and tames oxen, in Vedic the bull grows. Chance co-occurrence.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_12_Movses_Khor ed. page 1854 - PDF page 112 (word id 16231) (w2/2)
near_miss.lead: naming after father/brother (nafn/kalla ~ anown/kočʻem, bróðir ~ ełbayr)
near_miss.why_not: Snorri on kinship kennings, against eponymous place names in Movses. Different practices, generic vocabulary.
Norse has no 'golden oars'; gold and rowing occur in separate clauses of a metrical example. A golden boat is a generic image of opulence.

near_miss.lead: sól ~ sū́rya (eye to the sun, breath to the wind)
near_miss.why_not: The Norse pivot shares only 'sun', in a kenning, and the RV and AV witnesses are one branch. Nothing to claim.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 940 - PDF page 420 (word id 44005)
near_miss.lead: tvenn ... á tungu ~ duplicem ... linguam (twofold + tongue)
near_miss.why_not: Norse means abundant matter for poems (by twos and threes) on the tongue; Plautus means a snake's forked, flattering tongue. Different idioms; the Armenian is a golden tongue among the gifts.

near_miss.lead: myrkt af nótt ~ мрклој ноћи мрака / ноћи ... мрака (*mergʷ- 'dark' with *nókʷts)
near_miss.why_not: Cognate pair, and 'myrkt af nótt' is a stock saga phrase (about 20 hits in Menota and IcePaHC). But Vuk has only two hits, OE has no 'mirce niht' in the corpora, and 'dark night' is the most generic of collocations. I would not defend inheritance over independent use of the shared Germanic-Slavic word for 'dark'.
Father and mother are a universal pair; in Rígsþula they are the couple's names, and in the MBh one item in a list of five to be honoured.
The Third Grammatical Treatise depends on Latin grammar (Priscian), and 'tongue as rudder' is from James 3. Any match is learned transmission and generic phonetics, not inheritance.

error.correct_reading: ól, 3sg pret. of ala 'bear, give birth' (*h₂el- 'nourish')
error.evidence: Rígsþula birth formula 'Jóð ól Amma', with the subject following the verb; 'ale' makes no sense.
'snekkja heila' = 'ship of the brain', in a list of head kennings.
'bǫnd ollu því' = 'the gods caused that'; the dative því is governed by valda.

error.correct_reading: hattar, gen. sg. of hǫttr 'hat, hood' (helmet kenning herians hattar 'Óðinn's hat')
error.evidence: Snorri's gloss in the following unit explains the half-stanza as an axe kenning involving the helmet (sút hjálmsins).
